Presumably a full and correct theory of human psychology would explain all that. But that is centuries away. Today we are concerned to come up with a theory that lets us make predictions.

How do we compare theories? If theory T1 makes predictions that come true 60% of the time and theory T2 makes predictions that come true 40% of the time, we say that T1 is better than T2. But 60% is still shit. So the proponents of T2 don't just give up and switch to T1. They try tweaking T2. They've got a dream that T2.1 will be right 70% of the time. There is still everything to play for. The proponents of T1 know this; they are also trying to tweak T1 so that T1.1 will be right 80% of the time.

Over the years there is a two way traffic. Researchers abandoning T2 in favour of T1, obviously. But also intellectual journeys the other way, as proponents of T1 get sick of being stuck at 60% and start thinking: I've got a bright idea for T2.2 that will get it up to 70%

Lurking behind all this farting about is the curse of dimensionality. You can calibrate your theory on training data, and test it on test data (that is, freshly gathered data, not part of the training data). That is your forecast accuracy. It is easier to just look at how well your theory works on the training data. Call that the hindecast accuracy (not standard terminology). Adding bells and whistles to your theory lets you improve the hindecast accuracy without limit. With enough adjustments and enhancements it will be perfectly accurate. Forecast accuracy doesn't work like that. For subtle reasons, as you add extra features to your theory you reach a point where the forecast accuracy gets worse. Was the addition false, or have you run out of data?

Now we can say where simplified models, such the idea that humans are utility calculators, come from. Since we are in the early days of economics as a science we need simple models to avoid trashing our forecast accuracy and we need non-zero forecast accuracy to get clues as to whether our theorising is going in the right direction.

What bells and whistles might we add next? I suggest random splash and learning from experience. Picturing a human as some kind of idealised utility calculator is a bit like picturing a d6 as being marked with three and a half spots on each of the six sides. That works pretty well for the average roll. It predicts that the result of rolling a d6 ten times is 35. Actual results look like 42,28,36,38,33,30,28,26,30,35,...

It is hard to say if "all3.5" is a good theory or a bad theory. You might trying remembering actual rolls, perhaps 3,5,3,4,3,6 and decide that there are three 3's a four, a five, and a six. That theory gives you a worse prediction of the average, 4 instead of 3.5, but it does give you some random splash. Then again, it gives you a poor prediction of random splash, suggesting that ten rolls will never total less than 30.
